{{Short description|Survey methodology process}}
{{distinguish|Poisson disk sampling}}
In [[survey methodology]], '''Poisson sampling''' (sometimes denoted as ''PO sampling''<ref name="sarndal1992" />{{rp|61}}) is a [[sampling (statistics)|sampling]] process where each element of the [[statistical population|population]] is subjected to an [[statistical independence|independent]] [[Bernoulli trial]] which determines whether the element becomes part of the sample.<ref name="sarndal1992">{{cite book
 |title = Model Assisted Survey Sampling
 |author=Carl-Erik Sarndal |author2=Bengt Swensson |author3=Jan Wretman
 |isbn= 978-0-387-97528-3
 |year = 1992
}}</ref>{{rp|85}}<ref>Ghosh, Dhiren, and Andrew Vogt. "Sampling methods related to Bernoulli and Poisson Sampling." Proceedings of the Joint Statistical Meetings. American Statistical Association Alexandria, VA, 2002. [http://www.asasrms.org/Proceedings/y2002/Files/JSM2002-001080.pdf (pdf)]</ref>

Each element of the population may have a different probability of being included in the sample (<math>\pi_i</math>). The probability of being included in a sample during the drawing of a single sample is denoted as the ''first-order [[inclusion probability]]'' of that element (<math>p_i</math>). If all first-order inclusion probabilities are equal, Poisson sampling becomes equivalent to [[Bernoulli sampling]], which can therefore be considered to be a special case of Poisson sampling.

The name conveys that the number of samples leads to a [[Poisson binomial distribution]], which can approximate the [[Poisson distribution]] (via [[Le Cam's theorem]]).<ref>David B (https://stats.stackexchange.com/users/634/david-b), How can I efficiently model the sum of Bernoulli random variables?, URL (version: 2023-04-29): https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/5347</ref>

== A mathematical consequence of Poisson sampling ==

Mathematically, the first-order [[inclusion probability]] of the ''i''th element of the population is denoted by the symbol <math>\pi_i</math> and the second-order inclusion probability that a pair consisting of the ''i''th and ''j''th element of the population that is sampled is included in a sample during the drawing of a single sample is denoted by <math>\pi_{ij}</math>.

The following relation is valid during Poisson sampling when <math>i\neq j</math> (i.e., [[Independence (probability theory)|Independence]]):

:<math> \pi_{ij} = \pi_{i} \times \pi_{j}.</math>

<math>\pi_{ii}</math> is defined to be <math>\pi_i</math>.
